finding: §3.3 mandates that an unrecognized effective `review_converge_on` value is rejected as a *usage* error (exit 2) 'by every command that consumes the effective value (tp review/tp audit --status/--record)' regardless of which layer holds it — explicitly including `.tp/config.json` and the environment. But tp's exit-code table reserves exit 2 for command-line usage errors, exit 1 for validation, and exit 3 for file errors. When `tp review --status` fails only because a committed `.tp/config.json` (or an env var) carries a bad value, the operator's command invocation is correct; the fault is a config/validation problem, not a usage one. Routing all of these to exit 2 conflates a file/config-sourced validation failure with a malformed-invocation error, silently bending the exit-code invariant the spec never says it is changing. The parity claim 'the same way other workflow-field validation reports' also cuts against the table's 1=validation slot. Test 17 hard-codes the same exit-2 expectation, so the drift is pinned into acceptance.
suggestion: Split by source: keep exit 2 (usage) only for `tp set --workflow review_converge_on=<bad>` at write time, where the bad value is a command-line argument; for a consuming command (`tp review`/`tp audit --status`/`--record`) that reads the effective value from `.tp/config.json`, env, or a task override, reject with exit 1 (validation) — or exit 3 for the file layer — matching the exit-code table. Update §3.3 and Test 17 accordingly, or, if exit 2 is deliberate for all layers, state explicitly that this release widens the exit-code contract so an invalid config-sourced value is classified as usage.

finding: §3.3 names `tp audit --status`/`--record` in the list of commands that 'consume the effective value' of `review_converge_on` and must reject an unrecognized one as a usage error (exit 2); Test 17 reinforces this with 'by every consuming command'. But §4.4 and §10.4 state audit convergence is severity-blind, adds no `audit_converge_on`, and has no relationship to `review_converge_on` at all. An implementer cannot tell whether the `tp audit` command path must load and validate a review-only field it never otherwise reads: if it must, `tp audit` surprisingly fails on an invalid value that never affects it; if it must not, §3.3's explicit list and Test 17 are wrong. The buildable behavior (wire validation into audit or not) is left to guess.
suggestion: State explicitly whether `tp audit` consumes/validates `review_converge_on`. Either drop `tp audit` from the §3.3 consuming-commands list (audit never reads the field, so it should not error on it, matching §4.4/§10.4), or state that audit validates it only because it loads the shared workflow config and say so — and reconcile Test 17's 'every consuming command' to name the review commands only.

finding: Branch 3's compound directive embeds a non-angle-bracket placeholder, `tp set --workflow checks='[…]'`, but §8.2's placeholder-resolution paragraph resolves ONLY `<spec>`, `<base>`, and `<file>`, and says nothing about the `[…]` checks-array content. Test 14 asserts branch 3 'names the compound register-a-check-then-run-the-next-round directive' without pinning the emitted string. Two engineers write contradictory assertions: one expects tp to substitute the concrete recurring class(es) from `mechanize_candidates` into the JSON array (since branch 3 reads that same array), the other expects the literal `[…]` to survive verbatim (mirroring how `<file>` stays literal). No deterministic pass/fail test on the branch-3 next_action string can be written.
suggestion: In §8.2's resolution paragraph, state explicitly whether the branch-3 `checks='[…]'` placeholder is (a) filled with the concrete `mechanize_candidates` class name(s) tp read, or (b) emitted as a literal `[…]` template like `<file>`. Then have Test 14 assert the exact expected substring for the branch-3 directive.

finding: Residual phrasing from the round-10 removal of the persisted-clean-flag machinery. The clause "the live recompute never trusts a stored clean boolean when per-finding severity is present" scopes the distrust with "when per-finding severity is present", which implies a stored clean boolean exists and could be trusted when severity is absent. The same paragraph then states there is "no separate legacy stored-flag fallback" and, for the severity-less case, "no stored flag to read back", and Test 5 says cleanliness is computed "with no stored clean flag consulted". Since the simplification removed the stored flag entirely, the conditional qualifier presupposes an entity that no longer exists and mildly contradicts the surrounding absolute statements.
suggestion: Drop the conditional qualifier so the sentence asserts the flag is gone unconditionally, e.g. "because the live recompute reads cleanliness from the round's recorded findings rather than any stored clean flag" — removing "when per-finding severity is present", which is the last textual trace of the removed machinery.

finding: §3.3 gives two rules that conflict for a non-winning write: 'Validation applies to the *effective* (winning) value' (so an invalid value in a lower, non-winning layer does not error — restated in Test 17), yet 'The rejection is raised ... by `tp set --workflow` at write time'. When a higher-precedence layer (e.g. env or a task override) already holds a valid value, does `tp set --workflow review_converge_on=<invalid>` — writing a losing layer — fail at write time (validate the value being written) or succeed (because the effective winning value is still valid)? An implementer must choose one, and the two sentences point opposite ways.
suggestion: Pin the write-time behavior: either `tp set --workflow` always validates the literal value it is about to persist regardless of whether that layer wins (recommended — write-time validation normally guards the value being written), or it validates only when the written layer would win. State it and align Test 17 accordingly.

finding: §8.4 retains next_action under --compact, justifying it as "the command that changes the agent's very next call." But the strings §8.2 actually defines are multi-clause procedural sentences that re-narrate the loop the agent's skill/workflow already prescribes — e.g. "run the next review round: spawn the panel, merge, then tp review <spec> --record <file>" and "revise the spec to address the blocking findings, then run the next review round." On the --compact path, whose entire contract is Minimal Tokens (P3), the narration ("spawn the panel, merge, then") is bytes the agent does not need to make its next call; only the runnable atom (tp review <spec> --record <file>) or the shortest directive feeds the decision. The compact-retention rationale treats next_action as a command, but what is emitted is prose.
suggestion: Under --compact, trim next_action to the runnable command atom (or the shortest directive where no command exists), dropping the procedural narration the agent already knows; keep the fuller sentence only in full (non-compact) output. Alternatively, split the field so the command portion is what survives compaction.
